statement: The Commission states that European Business Wallets "could unlock another EUR 150 billion in savings for businesses each year", assuming broad uptake ("up to").
caveat: The FAQ words the condition as "if all companies take up"; the impact assessment uses 75% of economic operators and 100% of public bodies. The figure is not a GDP effect.

statement: At 75% adoption the impact assessment estimates total direct benefits of around EUR 169 billion per year: about EUR 14 billion for public sector bodies and EUR 155 billion for economic operators. It calls this "the estimated upper bound of potential benefits".
caveat: The press release figure of EUR 150 billion matches the economic-operator upper bound of EUR 154.45 billion (Table 9) rounded down.

statement: At 100% adoption by economic operators and public bodies the impact assessment gives about EUR 225 billion (EUR 19 billion public bodies, EUR 206 billion economic operators).
caveat: Full-adoption scenario; a theoretical ceiling. The same table appears in the explanatory memorandum of COM(2025) 838.

statement: Minimum direct benefit across the adoption ranges: EUR 58.42 billion (public bodies EUR 3.10 billion, economic operators EUR 55.32 billion); maximum EUR 168.79 billion.
caveat: Small survey samples; see limitations.

statement: Scope of the estimate: 32,721,957 economic operators (94.2% microenterprises, 5.6% SMEs, 0.2% corporates) and 95,825 public sector bodies (95,068 local administrative units and 757 central, regional, national and EU bodies).
Annual direct benefit per entity used in the model: microenterprise EUR 4,000; SME EUR 42,250; corporate EUR 97,300; average public sector body about EUR 199,600.
caveat: Averages across heterogeneous segments.

statement: Costs at 75% adoption: economic operators over EUR 45 billion in year 1 (about EUR 25 billion one-off plus EUR 21 billion recurring), then about EUR 21 billion per year; public bodies EUR 7.33 billion in year 1 (EUR 6.18 billion one-off, EUR 1.15 billion recurring). Per entity one-off and annual: micro EUR 620 and 500; SME EUR 2,600 and 5,000; corporate EUR 180,000 and 50,000.
caveat: The source text is inconsistent for economic-operator costs (a later passage gives nearly EUR 61 billion); not resolved here.

statement: Net direct benefit in the preferred adoption range: maximum EUR 115.97 billion in year 1 and EUR 147.22 billion in year 2; minimum about EUR 6 billion in year 1 and about EUR 37 billion in year 2. At the lowest adoption range (10%) the minimum net is about minus EUR 6 billion in year 1 and plus EUR 4 billion in year 2.
caveat: The lowest range "should not be interpreted as a minimum adoption scenario".

statement: Indirect benefits, stated as minimum quantifiable: trust in digital transactions EUR 16.66 billion, fraud reduction EUR 4.96 billion, data quality EUR 1.35 billion, resource reallocation and cross-border expansion EUR 0.45 billion.
caveat: Totals are inconsistent inside the document (EUR 23.42 billion in the table, EUR 26.81 billion in the text); some overlap with direct benefits may occur.

statement: The impact assessment lists its own limitations: limited public cost data, no comparable benchmarks, hard-to-forecast licensing fees, reliance on averages, a small number of survey responses (24 public bodies, 38 economic operators), and adoption assumptions that may be affected by political, technical or behavioural factors.

The Digital Package press release separates two figures: simplification measures estimated to save up to EUR 5 billion in administrative costs by 2029, and the European Business Wallets, which could unlock up to EUR 150 billion per year. The EUR 5 billion belongs to the Digital Omnibus, not the wallets.
caveat: Quoting EUR 5 billion and EUR 150 billion together as one figure would be wrong.

statement: A figure of EUR 37.5 billion recurring savings for SMEs that is often quoted could not be found in the press release, the FAQ, the "EBW in a nutshell" page or the impact assessment. The nearest official number is about EUR 37 billion net in year 2 (minimum, preferred adoption range).
caveat: Treat the SME figure as untraceable until a primary source is produced.

statement: Academic evidence on digital government and firm productivity: a difference-in-differences study of Chinese listed firms (2010-2020) finds an average increase in corporate total factor productivity of about 5%.
caveat: Listed firms only and China-specific: weak transferability to EU SMEs. Shows the direction of the effect, not an EU number.

statement: Cost per entity in the impact assessment model: one-off EUR 620 (micro), EUR 2,600 (SME), EUR 180,000 (corporate); annual licensing and maintenance EUR 500, EUR 5,000 and EUR 50,000. One-off items: training and onboarding, activation and IT implementation, contracting.
caveat: Training uses EUR 33.5 per hour from a 2018 German survey. The corporate IT figure draws on a vendor-commissioned study. The SME and corporate licence figures have no stated market source in the passages read.

statement: Stand-alone services for self-employed persons and sole traders (using their EUDI Wallet instead of a full Business Wallet): estimated annual recurring costs of EUR 45 for the new communications channel, EUR 150-200 for electronic signatures, EUR 350-400 for seals and EUR 235-285 for timestamps, for about 100 items.
caveat: The text says "new communications channel"; reading it as the qualified electronic registered delivery channel is an inference. The price is for self-employed persons and sole traders, not companies.

statement: The impact assessment found a licence price range of EUR 50 to 500 per year for basic wallet functions and a limited volume of transactions, and notes that prices vary with business needs and market dynamics.
caveat: The micro-company figure of EUR 500 is the top of this range.

statement: Per entity, annual maximum direct benefit against annual cost in year 2: micro EUR 4,000 against EUR 500; SME EUR 42,250 against EUR 5,000; corporate EUR 97,300 against EUR 50,000. The benefit values are described as potential maximum annual savings.
caveat: The comparison is derived here from two source tables, not stated in the source. The benefit figures are a theoretical upper bound; the ratio is therefore best-case.

statement: The impact assessment quotes the EIB Investment Report 2024/2025: regulatory compliance costs account for about 1.8% of turnover for firms and 2.5% for small and mid-size companies.
caveat: Primary EIB source not yet checked; value taken as quoted by the Commission.

statement: The impact assessment states that 55% of SMEs flagged administrative burden as their greatest challenge to remaining competitive, citing BusinessEurope 2025.
caveat: The cited source is a trade association, not an official statistic. The figure is not in the Call for Evidence, contrary to some secondary reports.

statement: Quoting the EIB Investment Report, the impact assessment states that about 86% of EU firms employ staff specifically for regulatory compliance and 28% of SMEs say more than 10% of their staff manage compliance.
caveat: Primary EIB source not yet checked.

statement: The Call for Evidence contains no savings figure and no 55% or turnover-share figure; its only number is a loss of "near EUR 2 trillion" in annual global economic value, without a stated source, and it says further research is needed to quantify financial savings.
caveat: Several secondary reports attribute the SME burden figures to the Call for Evidence; those attributions are not supported by the document.

statement: The European Council set a 35% SME burden-reduction target in March 2025. The impact assessment says the wallets deliver savings in line with or above that target; its maximum direct benefit at 100% adoption is EUR 200.77 billion per year (EUR 123.35 billion micro, EUR 77.42 billion SMEs).
caveat: The impact assessment states that the percentage depends on the baseline used.

statement: The impact assessment names barriers for companies: costs fall disproportionately on SMEs and micro firms that lack legal, IT or compliance departments; limited traceability of the EUDI Wallet makes integration with existing business processes (ERP, KYC) difficult; interoperability barriers and paper formalities remain.
FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center 2024: business email compromise accounted for 21,442 complaints and USD 2,770,151,146 in reported losses; all complaint types together USD 16.6 billion.
caveat: US data, not EU; no split by company size.

statement: Europol IOCTA 2025 and 2026 name business email compromise and CEO fraud as uses of stolen business data but give no euro loss figure; no EU-level company loss figure from Europol, ECB, EBA or ENISA could be traced.
caveat: Company-level fraud losses in the EU are not quantified in the sources found.

statement: Eurostat: 46.45% of EU enterprises used ERP software applications in 2025.
caveat: Relevant because ERP integration is the main driver of corporate implementation cost; size-class breakdown not extracted.

statement: The impact assessment does not quantify KYB or supplier onboarding cost per case, time to onboard, the cost of paper or PDF certificate exchange, or key-management cost, and gives no euro figure for company losses from impersonation or invoice fraud.
caveat: These items need primary company data or additional official studies.

statement: Evidence from related digitisation: computerised VAT invoicing in China raised VAT payments and productivity among large manufacturers (NBER Working Paper 24414); e-procurement in India and Indonesia improved quality and reduced delays without lower prices (Lewis-Faupel et al. 2016); VAT e-invoicing in Peru increased reported sales and purchases of small firms in the first year (Bellon et al. 2022, effect sizes not extracted).
caveat: None of these studies measures savings from business wallets, e-signatures or verifiable credentials; no peer-reviewed quantification of SME savings from them was found.

statement: Full-adoption table in the explanatory memorandum of COM(2025) 838: at 100% adoption by 95,825 public sector bodies and 32,721,957 economic operators, annual benefits of EUR 224.95 billion, costs of EUR 67.99 billion in year 1 and EUR 28.38 billion in year 2, net benefits of EUR 156.96 billion in year 1 and EUR 196.57 billion in year 2.
caveat: Full adoption by everyone is not a forecast; the memorandum states that net benefits depend on usage. Overlaps with the sector estimates below, which count the same processes; do not add them.

statement: Digital Product Passport: the Commission estimates the cost of setting up the central European digital product passport registry at around EUR 8 million one-off and at least EUR 1 million per year for maintenance.
basis: one-off, plus EUR 1 m per year
caveat: Public cost, not the cost for businesses; the annex states that business costs depend on the product-specific measures.

statement: Digital Product Passport: the impact assessment estimates the additional costs of a further 30 product-specific sustainability measures at EUR 30 to 60 billion per year when fully incurred, and says benefits are likely to be larger.
caveat: Covers all sustainable-product requirements, not the passport alone. No official quantification of the passport compliance cost per company was found.

statement: Data spaces and data contracts: the Digital Omnibus staff working document models savings of about EUR 1 billion from re-negotiating at least 100,000 contracts at an average cost of about EUR 10,000, and cites a study that large firms spend around EUR 1 million per year on data-management agreements.
caveat: About data-contract rules rather than organisation identity; included as the closest official quantification for data-space participation.

statement: Data Act impact assessment, as summarised secondarily: additional GDP of about EUR 270 billion by 2028, of which up to EUR 196.7 billion per year from data access and EUR 7.1 billion per year from cloud switching.
caveat: Not read in the original; the same source calls a related stakeholder cost estimate a considerable overestimation.

statement: No official, quantified cost of KYB, supplier qualification or onboarding into a data space was found. Subsidy caps in a Catena-X programme (up to EUR 15,000 for onboarding) are programme material, not measured costs.
caveat: Needs primary data from participants or an additional official study.

statement: Customs: the impact assessment puts economic operators' cost of complying with customs formalities in the EU at EUR 27.4 billion per year; the preferred option yields savings of EUR 40 billion over 15 years (average EUR 2.67 billion per year), or EUR 27 billion net after offsetting extra duties, excluding IT-cost savings that could not be quantified.
caveat: 15-year horizon; the Data Hub costs are modelled separately.

statement: Trade documents: an OECD analysis associates a 10% improvement in trade-facilitation indicators in four areas, including automation and streamlined documentation, with 18% higher global exports (37% with domestic regulatory reforms), and cites UNESCAP for a 0.8% reduction in trade costs per 10% increase in paperless-trade reform implementation.
caveat: The paper stresses that process streamlining has to come before digitalisation.

statement: E-invoicing and VAT (ViDA impact assessment): e-invoicing-related savings of EUR 1.9 billion (lower option) to EUR 14.5 billion (maximal option); for digital reporting requirements, option 4a has costs of EUR 13.5 billion, benefits of EUR 152.4 billion and net EUR 138.9 billion, option 4b costs of EUR 46.9 billion, benefits of EUR 278.1 billion and net EUR 231.1 billion.
caveat: Time basis of the e-invoicing table not checked; options are policy designs, not adoption levels.

statement: The ViDA impact assessment cites a VAT gap of EUR 134 billion and about EUR 40 to 60 billion of VAT fraud as the fiscal rationale for stronger verification of businesses.
caveat: Context for the value of reliable business identification, not a saving attributable to wallets.

statement: Reporting obligations: the Digital Omnibus expects at least EUR 5 billion of administrative cost savings for businesses by 2029 and EUR 1 billion for public authorities, with up to EUR 1.34 billion per year recurring and EUR 1.04 billion one-off quantified for businesses.
caveat: These are Omnibus savings and are not the wallet savings; the press release keeps the two figures apart.

statement: Single entry point for incident reports (NIS2, DORA and other acts): about EUR 440 per incident (12 staff hours), 1.18 incidents per entity per year, at least 160,000 NIS2 entities; total reporting cost EUR 83.07 million per year and savings of about EUR 41.5 million per year, a lower bound that excludes GDPR. The Omnibus describes the single entry point as interoperable with European Business Wallets and names it as one use case for them.
caveat: The SME Panel put the overall cost of reporting an incident at EUR 500 to 35,000; stakeholders could not produce a quantified estimate. ENISA development cost about EUR 6 million.

statement: Academic context: a major economics survey finds that digitisation lowers the costs of search, replication, transport, tracking and verification; a qualitative study of traceability identifies capability, collaboration, technology maturity, governance and leadership as success factors; a cost-profit model for digital product passports has been applied to battery repurposing.
caveat: Summaries taken from citation data and search results; none estimates the value of organisation identity. Verify against the papers before relying on them.
